title: Fair Housing & Civil Rights Law (Federal + California)
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: When federal and California fair housing protections differ, California real estate practice generally follows:
options: The more protective standard, typically California's broader list
rationales: Federal law alone would omit California-specific protections.
Correct. The more protective standard generally controls in California.
Agent preference does not determine which law applies.
Local ordinances may add further protections but do not replace this rule.

questions.stem: Which is a California-specific protected class not guaranteed the same way under the federal FHA?
rationales: Race is a federal protected class.
Correct. Source of income, including housing vouchers, is a notable California-specific expansion.
National origin is a federal protected class.
Disability is a federal protected class.

questions.stem: Refusing to rent to a qualified applicant because they intend to pay with a housing voucher is:
options: Permitted, since vouchers are not guaranteed income
rationales: Voucher-based refusal is not permitted in California.
Correct. Treating voucher income differently from other lawful income is discriminatory under California law.
This is specifically a California-law issue as much as federal.
Advance disclosure of an intent to discriminate does not make it lawful.

questions.stem: Disparate treatment requires:
options: A neutral policy with unequal statistical effect
Intentional differential treatment because of a protected characteristic
rationales: That describes disparate impact, not treatment.
Correct. Disparate treatment is intentional discrimination.
Disparate treatment requires intent, unlike disparate impact.
It can occur through unwritten conduct, not only written policy.

questions.stem: Disparate impact liability can arise from:
options: Only explicit statements naming a protected class
A facially neutral policy with a statistically disproportionate discriminatory effect and no defensible business necessity
rationales: Explicit statements are more typical of disparate treatment.
Correct. Disparate impact targets neutral policies with discriminatory effect, absent a valid business necessity.
Intent is not required for disparate impact.
Screening policies, not just advertising, can trigger disparate impact analysis.

questions.stem: A property manager sets a minimum credit score requirement well above what is needed to ensure ability to pay rent, with no alternative proof-of-payment option. This practice most directly raises a concern under:
rationales: There is no stated intent to discriminate, so disparate treatment is not the primary theory here.
Correct. A facially neutral criterion set well above business necessity can have a disparate statistical effect.
The parol evidence rule is unrelated.
The Statute of Frauds is unrelated.

questions.stem: Steering is best described as:
options: Denying loans based on neighborhood racial composition
Directing prospects toward or away from neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic
Inducing panic selling based on demographic change
rationales: That describes redlining.
Correct. Steering directs prospects based on a protected characteristic.
That describes blockbuking.
Credit checks alone are not steering.

questions.stem: Redlining is best described as:
options: Denying or limiting financial services based on an area's racial or ethnic composition
rationales: That describes steering, not redlining.
Correct. Redlining denies or limits services based on area demographics rather than individual creditworthiness.
It is unrelated to boundary disputes.
It is unrelated to zoning variances.

questions.stem: Blockbuking involves:
options: Inducing panic selling by suggesting protected-class residents will lower property values
rationales: Correct. Blockbuking exploits fear of demographic change to induce panic sales.
It is unrelated to legal descriptions.
It is unrelated to foreclosure.
It is unrelated to dual agency.

questions.stem: An agent tells a family, based on assumptions about the neighborhood's demographics, 'I think you'd be happier somewhere else.' This is most accurately an example of:
rationales: This is not legitimate neutral advice; it is based on protected-class assumptions.
Correct. Directing prospects based on assumed characteristics is steering, even when framed helpfully.
This is unrelated to disability accommodation.
This does not involve inducing panic selling.

questions.stem: A reasonable accommodation is:
options: A required change to a rule, policy, or practice
Always paid for by the tenant
Optional even for legitimate disability needs
rationales: That describes a reasonable modification.
Correct. Accommodation involves policy/rule changes, generally at the landlord's expense.
Accommodations are generally provided at the landlord's expense, not the tenant's.
It is a required obligation, not optional, when legitimate and reasonable.

questions.stem: A reasonable modification is:
options: A change to a rule or policy
A physical structural change, often at the tenant's expense
The same thing as a reasonable accommodation
rationales: That describes a reasonable accommodation.
Correct. Modifications are physical changes, and the tenant often bears the cost though the landlord must permit it.
Landlords generally must permit reasonable modifications.
They are legally distinct concepts, though related.

questions.stem: A tenant with legitimate documentation requests an emotional support animal in a building with a strict no-pets policy and breed restrictions. The landlord should generally:
options: Apply the no-pets policy and breed restriction as written
Treat this as a reasonable accommodation request and grant it absent a direct threat or fundamental alteration
Charge a pet deposit and pet rent
Deny it automatically since it is a dog
rationales: The no-pets policy and breed restrictions do not apply to a qualifying assistance animal.
Correct. This is an accommodation request, generally required to be granted when legitimate.
Assistance animals cannot be charged pet deposits or pet rent.
Automatic denial based on species or breed is not the correct standard.

questions.stem: An assistance/support animal for fair housing purposes is treated as:
options: A pet subject to standard pet policies
Not a pet, and not subject to pet deposits or breed restrictions
Only allowed with special written permission from HUD
rationales: It is not treated as an ordinary pet.
Correct. Fair housing law excludes qualifying assistance animals from pet policies, deposits, and breed restrictions.
No separate HUD permission process is required for this protection to apply.
It is not prohibited; it must generally be accommodated.

questions.stem: Federal fair housing complaints are investigated primarily by:
rationales: The IRS is unrelated to fair housing enforcement.
Correct. HUD investigates federal Fair Housing Act complaints.
The assessor is unrelated to fair housing enforcement.
The DRE handles licensee discipline but is not the primary federal enforcement body.

questions.stem: California's state agency enforcing FEHA and Unruh Act housing protections is:
rationales: HUD is the federal enforcement agency.
Correct. California's Civil Rights Department (formerly DFEH) enforces FEHA and Unruh Act housing protections.
DFPI regulates financial services, not fair housing enforcement.
The DRE handles real estate licensing, not the primary fair housing enforcement body.

questions.stem: A fair housing tester who never genuinely intended to rent a unit but posed as a prospect to detect discrimination:
options: Has no legal standing to sue
Has legal standing to sue, and their evidence is generally admissible
Can only report findings to the press
Must disclose their tester status before visiting a property
rationales: Testers do have recognized legal standing.
Correct. Testers have standing to sue, and their evidence is generally admissible despite lacking genuine rental intent.
Testers can pursue formal legal remedies, not only press reporting.
Testers are not required to disclose their status in advance to be effective and have standing.

questions.stem: Marketing language describing a listing as 'perfect for a young family' raises a compliance concern because it:
options: Is always illegal regardless of context
Edges toward familial-status-coded language that should be avoided
Only matters for rental listings, never sales
rationales: Context matters, but this phrasing carries real risk and should be avoided.
Correct. It signals a preferred resident type tied to a protected characteristic.
Effective marketing can and should avoid such language.
Advertising rules apply to both sales and rental marketing.

questions.stem: Remedies for a fair housing violation can include:
options: Actual damages, penalties, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees, plus possible license discipline for a real estate licensee
No remedies unless HUD sues personally
rationales: This undersells the range of available remedies.
Correct. Multiple remedies exist, and licensees face independent license discipline risk.
Private lawsuits are also available without requiring HUD to be the plaintiff.
Criminal prosecution is not the typical primary remedy in most fair housing cases.

questions.stem: Good intent is:
options: A complete defense to both disparate treatment and disparate impact claims
A defense to disparate treatment but not to disparate impact
A defense to disparate impact but not disparate treatment
rationales: Good intent does not fully defeat disparate impact claims.
Correct. Lack of intent can defeat disparate treatment but does not excuse a discriminatory statistical effect under disparate impact.
This reverses the correct relationship.
Intent is relevant, particularly to disparate treatment claims.
